context: Convex subset of a real vector space, equivalent two-point and Minkowski-set formulations / two-point-convex-combination
editorial_note: The directly read ProofWiki Vector Space convex-set page explicitly presents both the two-vector closure condition and equivalent inclusion tC+(1-t)C⊆C in a vector space over R or C; this mathematical meaning specializes to a REAL vector space. The two formulations refer to the SAME convex subset, with each vector x,y arbitrary points in C and every REAL t∈[0,1]. The empty set is convex vacuously; both inclusion and quantified point versions hold for C=∅, supporting earlier conv(∅)=∅. A line segment between points is fully included exactly when the set is convex. Real scalars are required for [0,1] even if ambient complex scalar vector space is allowed on the source page; complex space can be regarded as a real vector space by restriction but is not the adopted source context here. Neither norm, closure/topological closedness, finite dimension, or connectedness is required. This meaning was a separately identified missing prerequisite for earlier convex-hull formulations, not read from original production mathDef. Source sections: Definition 1 all two-point real convex combinations, Definition 2 Minkowski convex combination inclusion, Line Segment equivalent geometric description
text: Let V be a vector space over ℝ and C⊆V. The subset C is convex if for every x,y∈C and t∈[0,1], the vector tx+(1−t)y belongs to C.

context: Nonnegative-index falling factorial for a real argument, with independently sourced zero case / finite-decreasing-product
editorial_note: ProofWiki's directly inspected Falling Factorial definition states the product for POSITIVE integer n, not n=0. Its independent Binomial Coefficient with Zero theorem was ALSO read and explicitly confirms the vacuous-product convention x^{underline 0}=1; MathWorld Falling Factorial separately agrees. The adopted mathematical meaning includes n∈N_0 using BOTH source locations as jointly documented evidence; it must never be falsely attributed to the positive-n definition page alone. This nonnegative extension supplies the k=0 term of the previously sourced Stirling polynomial identity. Falling factorial for n>0 is x(x−1)...(x−n+1), not the rising factorial x(x+1)...(x+n−1). Names like Pochhammer symbol and (x)_n have conflicting conventions, so the falling underline notation is explicit. No assumption x is an integer or n≤x; for arbitrary real x the polynomial product remains meaningful. Do not replace this definition with x!/(x−n)! without integer/domain conditions, because that factorial quotient may not exist for negative or nonintegral values. Source sections: Positive n falling factorial product, Vacuous n=0 product independently corroborated in Binomial Coefficient with Zero, Pochhammer naming conventions ambiguous
text: For x∈ℝ and n∈ℕ₀, define x^{\underline n}=∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(x−j), with the empty-product convention x^{\underline 0}=1. Thus for n≥1 it equals x(x−1)⋯(x−n+1).

context: Numeric equality-indicator Kronecker delta indexed by any set Γ, two equivalent formulations / numeric-case-definition
editorial_note: ProofWiki directly defines the numerical Kronecker delta as the equality test on Γ×Γ with values in {0,1}, and explicitly gives the Iverson bracket expression as another presentation. These are equivalent formulas in the SAME numeric meaning, which is directly applicable to the Stirling boundary S(n,0)=δ_{n,0}. For Γ empty the map has empty domain and is defined uniquely; for a nonempty Γ the diagonal maps to 1 and all unequal pairs to 0. The source ALSO separately gives a ring-with-unity valued Kronecker delta with distinguished 0_R and 1_R: that formulation is NOT added to the numeric meaning without specifying the output ring. The numeric version does not require Γ be an ordered, natural or finite set. δ_{a,b} is notation for a function of TWO indices; it should not be confused with Dirac delta distribution, partial derivatives or an arithmetic difference a−b. Source sections: Numbers: δ:Γ×Γ→{0,1} equality test, Also presented as Iverson bracket, Ring-valued delta is a distinct context not promoted
text: For any set Γ, the numerical Kronecker delta is δ:Γ×Γ→{0,1} defined by δ(a,b)=1 when a=b and δ(a,b)=0 when a≠b.

context: Bipartiteness for loopless simple undirected graph, cross-part and proper two-color criteria / cross-part-edges
editorial_note: ProofWiki explicitly defines a bipartite graph through vertex parts A and B with every edge joining DIFFERENT parts, and equivalently no within-part adjacent pair; it describes coloring the parts with two colors. This screen specializes to SIMPLE LOOPLESS UNDIRECTED graphs so unordered two-element edges suffice. A c:V→{0,1} two-coloring not necessarily onto is equivalent to a disjoint two-part cover by setting A=c^{-1}(0), B=c^{-1}(1). IMPORTANT: the phrase 'partition into two sets' may conventionally require nonempty blocks; graph bipartiteness cannot require both colors actually occur. Edgeless graphs on a nonempty V and the empty graph are bipartite, with one or both color classes empty. This editorial convention is explicit rather than a universal claim about definitions of partition. No finiteness or connectedness of G is required. Bipartite does not mean COMPLETE bipartite (all cross-part edges present); do not infer the stronger K_{m,n} property or a unique bipartition. An odd cycle prevents bipartiteness, but that theorem is not itself a separate definition here. Source sections: Definition graph with two vertex parts and cross-part edges, That is: no same-part adjacent vertices, Two-color depiction provides equivalent coloring criterion
text: A simple undirected graph G=(V,E) is bipartite if there are disjoint subsets A,B⊆V with A∪B=V and every edge {u,v}∈E has one endpoint in A and the other in B; either part may be empty.
